content.title: One Source of Truth and State Ownership
content.hook: A large application can contain many state values without having one giant global state object.
content.context:
The key principle is:

**For each piece of state, know who owns it.**

That owner is responsible for defining the current value and the rules for changing it.
goals: Master One Source of Truth and State Ownership: For each piece of state, know who owns it.

content.title: The problem with duplication
content.text:
Imagine:

```text
Header      → selectedAccount = "A"
Dashboard   → selectedAccount = "A"
Sidebar     → selectedAccount = "A"
```

If each area stores its own copy, what happens when the account changes?

You now have to keep three values synchronized.

content.title: Better
content.text:
Choose one source of truth:

```text
Account state
    ↓
Header
Dashboard
Sidebar
```

The consumers read the same underlying value.

content.question:
Two sibling components must always show the same selected tab.

Where should that state usually live?

options.text: In their closest useful shared owner

feedback.correct: Put shared state at the smallest owner that can coordinate every component that depends on it.
feedback.incorrect: Put shared state at the smallest owner that can coordinate every component that depends on it.

content.question:
A common overcorrection is lifting everything to the application root.

Imagine a tooltip that exists only inside one table row.

Does the whole application need to own whether the tooltip is open?

options.text:
No


The state should usually stay near the interaction that needs it.

feedback.correct:
Correct answer: B. No


The state should usually stay near the interaction that needs it.
feedback.incorrect:
Correct answer: B. No


The state should usually stay near the interaction that needs it.

content.title: State locality
content.text:
Think in terms of a ladder:

```text
One button
   ↓
One component
   ↓
One section
   ↓
One route
   ↓
Several routes
   ↓
Whole application
```

Move the state upward only when the requirement crosses another boundary.

content.title: Impossible combinations
content.text:
Suppose an application keeps:

```js
isLoading
isSuccess
hasError
```

What combinations might become awkward?

For example:

```text
isLoading = true
isSuccess = true
```

If those states should never happen together, the state structure itself is making invalid situations easy to create.

A better shape may be:

```js
status = "idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error"
```

Now the valid states are explicit.

content.question: Which state shape communicates a clearer set of possibilities?

options.text: Three unrelated booleans that can contradict each other
One status value representing the valid stages
Five copied values in different components
A value duplicated in local storage and state for no reason

feedback.correct: Correct answer: B. One status value representing the valid stages
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: B. One status value representing the valid stages

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: Good state architecture does two things:
**It gives each piece of state a clear owner.**
**It makes invalid combinations harder to represent.**
nextSteps: Take one screen with three or more related state variables. Identify the owner of each and look for any combinations that should be impossible.

Complete the checkpoint and explain the mechanism in your own words. A wrong first prediction is expected; the mastery signal is whether you can explain the result and handle a changed case after feedback.
